h1: Illinois HOA Lien & Foreclosure Threat Response Demand Letter
metaTitle: Illinois HOA Lien Foreclosure Demand Letter Tool
metaDescription: Generate an Illinois HOA lien or foreclosure threat response demand letter. Cite state law, demand validation, and protect your home from improper association action.
statuteCitation: 765 ILCS 605/9 (Illinois Condominium Property Act, lien for unpaid common expenses); 735 ILCS 5/9-104.1 (demand before a condominium eviction action); 765 ILCS 160/1-45 (Common Interest Community Association Act, finances)
deadline: At least 30 days to satisfy a written demand before a condominium association files an eviction (forcible entry and detainer) action (735 ILCS 5/9-104.1)
penalty: The demand and the attorney's fees it claims are open to court review in the eviction case (735 ILCS 5/9-104.1(a)); a demand that does not meet the statute can be challenged as a defense
introParagraph: If your Illinois homeowners association or condominium board has threatened to record a lien or foreclose on your property over unpaid assessments, you have important rights under state law. Illinois requires HOAs and condo associations to follow strict notice, accounting, and procedural rules before they can place a lien or pursue foreclosure. Many associations skip steps, miscalculate balances, or pile on improper fines, late fees, and attorney charges. A well-drafted demand letter citing the Illinois Condominium Property Act or the Common Interest Community Association Act can force your association to validate the debt, correct errors, and pause collection activity. Acting quickly—before a lien is recorded or a complaint is filed—often resolves the dispute without court intervention and preserves your credit and equity.
lawExplanation: Illinois regulates HOA and condominium collections through two primary statutes. The Illinois Condominium Property Act (765 ILCS 605), particularly Section 9, gives a condominium association a statutory lien on the unit for unpaid common expenses and unpaid fines, together with interest, late charges, reasonable attorney fees incurred enforcing the covenants, and costs of collection (765 ILCS 605/9(g)(1)). Notice of the lien may be recorded by the board, and once notice is recorded the lien may be foreclosed by an action brought in the board's name in the same manner as a mortgage of real property (765 ILCS 605/9(h)). The Common Interest Community Association Act (765 ILCS 160) covers common interest communities, but an association organized as an Illinois not-for-profit corporation that has 10 units or fewer, or annual budgeted assessments of $100,000 or less, is exempt unless it elects to be covered (765 ILCS 160/1-75(a)). Before filing an eviction (forcible entry and detainer) action against a condominium unit owner for unpaid assessments, the association must serve a written demand that gives the owner at least 30 days to satisfy it and sets out the amount claimed and the periods when the amounts were originally due; the amount may include regular or special assessments, late charges or interest, and attorney's fees for services incurred before the demand, and those fees are subject to court review (735 ILCS 5/9-104.1(a)). Common interest community associations that elect to use the same procedure follow the same rules (735 ILCS 5/9-102(a)(8); 735 ILCS 5/9-104.3). Illinois law limits what can be collected to the items the statute and your governing documents allow. Fines must be supported by notice and an opportunity to be heard under the association's bylaws. A demand that does not satisfy the statute can be challenged in the eviction case. Additionally, the federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act may apply when a third-party law firm sends collection demands, giving owners further validation rights. Knowing which statute governs your community—condo versus common interest community—determines exactly which notices and defenses apply.
letterStrategy: An effective Illinois HOA demand letter does three things: it formally disputes the alleged debt, demands a complete statutory accounting, and puts the association on notice of legal violations that could derail any lien or foreclosure action. Start by citing the specific statute that governs your community—765 ILCS 605/9 for condominiums or 765 ILCS 160 for common interest communities—and request a detailed itemization of every assessment, late fee, fine, and attorney charge claimed. Demand copies of the board resolutions authorizing late fees and fines, the meeting minutes showing proper adoption, and proof that hearing rights were provided before any fine was imposed. Identify any procedural defects: a demand for possession that gives less than 30 days or omits the amount claimed and the periods when it was due, unauthorized fees, or charges applied during a disputed period. If a third-party collector or law firm sent the threat, invoke FDCPA validation rights. Conclude with a clear demand: correct the ledger, withdraw improper charges, and refrain from recording a lien or filing suit while the dispute is being resolved. Offer to pay the legitimately owed balance upon receipt of corrected documentation. A letter like this creates a written record that often persuades boards and their attorneys to negotiate, accept a payment plan, or drop disputed charges rather than risk a contested case where they may lose the right to recover attorney's fees. Send it by certified mail and email to the association manager, board president, and any attorney of record.
proceduralNotes: Illinois condo associations typically pursue collection through forcible entry and detainer (eviction) proceedings in circuit court rather than small claims, because they seek possession plus money. The small claims limit in Illinois is $10,000, but most assessment disputes are filed as standard civil or forcible actions. A recorded condominium lien may be foreclosed in the same manner as a mortgage of real property (765 ILCS 605/9(h)), which brings in the Illinois Mortgage Foreclosure Law (735 ILCS 5/15-1101 et seq.). Owners generally have a redemption period and the right to cure by paying the full amount owed. Actions on written contracts are subject to a ten-year limitation (735 ILCS 5/13-206); whether that period governs a particular claim under a declaration depends on how the claim is framed. Always verify deadlines with current court rules or an Illinois attorney before relying on them.

faq.q: Can my Illinois HOA foreclose on my home for unpaid dues?
faq.a: A condominium association has a statutory lien for unpaid assessments (765 ILCS 605/9(g)(1)) that may be foreclosed after notice of the lien is recorded (765 ILCS 605/9(h)), and it may also pursue an eviction action under Article IX of the Code of Civil Procedure. Remedies of a common interest community association come from its declaration and, if it elects, the same eviction procedure (735 ILCS 5/9-102(a)(8)). The association must follow the notice and accounting requirements in the statute and your governing documents first. A demand letter challenging procedural defects or improper charges can often stop or delay collection and force negotiation.

faq.q: What notice must an Illinois HOA give before recording a lien?
faq.a: Before a condominium association files an eviction action for unpaid assessments, it must serve a written demand giving at least 30 days to pay, stating the amount claimed and when it was originally due (735 ILCS 5/9-104.1(a)). Your declaration, bylaws, or the association's collection policy may require additional notice. A demand that does not meet the statute can be challenged as a defense in the eviction case, and the attorney's fees claimed in the demand are subject to court review.

faq.q: Can I dispute fines and late fees on my HOA ledger?
faq.a: Yes. Fines must be authorized by your declaration or bylaws, properly adopted by the board, and imposed only after notice and an opportunity to be heard. Late fees must be reasonable and authorized in writing. Many Illinois owners successfully challenge fines that lack hearing documentation or late fees not adopted by board resolution. A demand letter requesting copies of the authorizing documents often results in disputed charges being removed from the account.

faq.q: Do I have to pay HOA attorney's fees added to my balance?
faq.a: Only reasonable fees actually incurred and authorized by your declaration or Illinois statute. Associations frequently inflate attorney charges or add fees for routine letters. You can demand itemized billing showing the work performed, the rate, and the time spent. Courts have reduced or denied excessive fee requests. If the association loses key procedural arguments, it may forfeit fee recovery entirely under Illinois law.

faq.q: Will sending a demand letter stop the foreclosure clock?
faq.a: A demand letter does not automatically pause foreclosure deadlines, but it creates a written dispute record that often prompts the association or its attorney to delay filing while issues are addressed. If the letter exposes notice defects or improper charges, the association may withdraw and re-issue notices, effectively resetting the timeline. Always send by certified mail, keep copies, and consult an Illinois attorney immediately if a complaint or lien has already been filed.
